I. 


THE ONE HUNDRED AND FIRST ANNUAL REPORT 
OF THE 
YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL 
FOR THE YEAR ENDING DECEMBER 31ST, 1952 


INTRODUCTION 


Your Board of Directors submits herewith the Annual 
Report of the Young Men's Christian Association of Montreal for 
the year ending December 31st, 1952, in accordance with the 
requirements of the Constitution. 

This report will deal with matters of general interest 
affecting the Montreal Association as a whole, as detailed reports 
of the various branches have already been submitted and approved 
at their respective annual meetings and are included in their own 
recordse 

On the world scene, the undeclared war in Korea con= 
tinued into its third year, Talk of truce also continued with 
slow progress towards armisticee 

In Canada, our national economy retained an expanding 
trende During the summer, the Canadian dollar attained a strong 
premium position among world currencies. Employment and wages 
were maintained at a high level. 

In our own Association, the first year of our second 
century was outstanding, with plans for city-wide expansion well 
under way. Towards the end of the year, our Montreal Y.M.C.A. 
engaged in a Capital Funds Campaign, the fifth in our history, 
in order that we might continue to meet the ever increasing needs 
of youth throughout the metropolitan area and in the Sir George 
Williams College and Schools, 

In September, we welcomed Fred Ge Hubbard as our new 
General Secretarye Associated with the Canadian Y.MeCeA. for the 
past thirty-two years, in Winnipeg, Toronto and Vancouver, he is 
the fifth General Secretary to be associated with the Montreal Y.M.C.A. 
since it was organized in 1851, 


Ile 


20 


OUR METROPOLITAN ORGANIZATION 


In Greater Montreal, the Association operates in 
and from eleven self-governing branches, the Sir George Williams 
College and Schools, three summer camps and a ski lodges 

Five branches are located in fully-equipped Y.M.C.Ae-~ 
owned buildings: Central, 1;1 Drummond Street; Notre Dame de 
Grace, 335 Hampton Avenue; International, 5550 Park Avenue; 
Southwestern, 1000 Gordon Avenue; Westmount, 585 Sherbrooke 
Street Weste 

Six branches make use of rented headquarters and 
facilities in communities located far from the Central building 
which contains the Association Metropolitan Offices: City Hall 
Avenue, 183 St. Catherine Street East; Lachine, 190-51st Avenue 

formerly Summerlea United Church); Point St. Charles, in Lorne 
School, 2387 Coleraine Street; Rosemount, in Nesbitt School, 
3001 Rosemount Blvd; Montreal East, in Montreal East School, 
123 St. Cyr Street; and Northmount, 927 Crevier Street, Ville St. 
Laurente 

Serving the entire metropolitan area, Sir George 
Williams College and Schools are located in the Central Association 
building on Drummond Street, and in five annexes in close proximity 
on Drummond and Stanley Streetse 

Camp Otoreke, for young men and women, is situated 
sixty-five miles north of Montreal, at Lake St. Joseph, near 
Stes Agathe des Monts in the Laurentians, on extensive island 
property owned by the Montreal Y.M.C.A. 

Kamp Kanawana, for boys 8 - 16 years of age, covers 
sixty acres of woodland and lakes, on Y.M.C.A. property, near Ste 
Sauveur in the Laurentians, fifty miles north of Montreale 

Camp Perrot, for boys and girls 10 ~ 16 years of Age, 
is located on forty acres of Y.M.C.A. land on De Perrot, facing 
Lake Ste Louis, in the St. Lawrence River, twenty-eight miles west 
of Montreal, A winter lodge, owned and operated by the Y.M.C.A+ as 
the Christieville Ski Club for young men and women is located sixty 


miles north of Montreal in the Laurentian Mountains.

PROGRAM 


Through program and personal services, the Y.M.C.A. 
seeks to accomplish its purpose of "building Christian personality 
and a Christian societye" Only insofar as this is being accom 
plished in the lives of individuals has our program significances 
A broad range of activities has been carried on during the year, 
in our attempt to interpret the three sides of our red triangle 
in terms of spirit, mind and body. Detailed summaries of all 
program activities are included in reports which have been presented 
at branch annual meetings for the eleven communities served by 
the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal. Hence this report deals only with the 
metropolitan aspects of our work, 


Clubs and Groups: 

he Y.M.C.A» program of self-governing clubs and 
groups is of utmost importance in the lives of its memberse In 
fellowship and purpose clubs, young people gain experience through 
assuming responsibilities which help them to become good citizens 
in a Christian democracy. In all, 875 clubs and interest groups 
recorded a total enrollment of 324143 different individuals. 

Forty-six of our purpose clubs have followed a 
nationally recognized pattern, These include seven Phalanx and 
Phiat Clubs for young men and women 18 - 25 yearsof ages; seventeen 
senior and three junior Hi-Y Clubs of students in eight High Schools, 
and twenty-six Gra-Y Clubs of boys and girls in seventeen Elementary 
Schools throughout the metropolitan areas Induction of members into 
these clubs requires a willingness on their part to attempt to live 
up to the club's stated Christian purposee Last year, 1019 young 
people were members, of which 50 per cent were high school boys and 
gi ri Se 

To share ideas with delegates from other clubs across 
Canada, twelve boys and girls represented Montreal Clubs at the 
Fifth National Hi-Y Assembly held at Gouchiching last summer, the 
largest Assembly in the history of the Hi-Y movement in Canadas 


IITs 


he 


PROGRAM (cont'd) 


So that our clubs might function efficiently through the school 
year, more than fifty boys and girls in executive positions 
attended a twomday Fall Officers Training Conference. In the 
Easter holiday period, a three-day Regional Eastern Ontario and 
Quebec Hi~Y Conference was held in Montreal. Two hundred and 
thirty delegates, 87 from out of town and 143 Montreal boys and 
girls attended the Conference which was planned by the Grand 
Chapters of Montreal Clubs, who chose the theme "Let's Look 
Aheade" 

Sixty-two other friendship clubs enrolled 1838 members, 
Included in these are neighbourhood (N-Y) Glubs of boys and girls, 
where clubs are formed of natural groups of children living within 
a neighbourhood. Parents form sponsoring groups for these clubs, 
and many meetings are regularly held in homes. This type of club 
is a recent trend in Y.M.C.A. program which is rapidly gaining 
popularity. 


Informal Education: 

Crafts and hobbies, especially in children's program, 
and lectures, forums and study groups have been given further 
emphasis in city-wide program. This trend is reflected in the 
Significant increase of attendances at these activities over the 
previous year. 2725 in 1952, as compared with 723095 in 1951). 

As winter program drew to a close, Central, Notre 
Dame de Grace and Southwestern Branches each planned Spring So= 
Ed programs of 6 ~ 8 weeks duration. These special series attracted 
large groups of young men and women. 

Sponsored by the Metropolitan Young Adults Committee, 
the third Annual Model United Nations Assembly was held in Budge 
Halle This educational project in international affairs attracted 
a number of groups of young people of colleges, churches and clubs, 
who took part in the three Assembly sessions, along with groups from 
Y.M.C.A+s branches and Sir George Williams College. A large audience 
followed the proceedings conducted in a manner to bring credit to 
the Association and the various youth groups participating.

Se 


PROGRAM (cont'd) 


International Branch continued to welcome New 
Canadianse Enrolled in its membership were people from more 
than forty nations, many of whom had been connected with the 
Y.M.C.A* or knew of its work in their native land. Year-round 
language classes have been held each week-day evening, with 
28,65) recorded attendances in graded classes, under the 
instruction of expert teachers. Employment and personal inter~ 
views have been significant services to new members, Copies 
of an outstanding address to New Canadians, delivered at a 
Citizenship Meeting were sent to all Y.M.C.A.'s throughout 
Canadae 

Our three libraries have been well used, with a 
book circulation of 34,966. Early issues of the "Montreal 
Witness" from 186 - 1900 were donated by the family of the 
late Fred E, Dougall as a valuable addition to the Canadiana 
of the Sir George Williams College Library. 


Health and Physical Fitness: 
Our city-wide physical program has been comprehensive, 


including formal classes and recreational clubse In addition 

to gymnasiums and swimming pools of our five building branches, 

we have made extensive use of outdoor and indoor facilities of 
thirteen schools in many communities. Many of our inter~branch 
athletic competitions have become established annual events. 

Notably among these were Basketball Jamborees for boys, monthly 
Progressive Swim Meets for boys and girls, gymnastic meets for 
young men and an athletic evening for young women. Intermediate 
Leaders Corps members of five branches met in conference, Many 
hundreds of parents and fricnds attended Annual Gymnastic Displays 
held at the close of the winter's programe Special Learn~to-Swim 
Campaigns for school children were held in each of the Yel.C.Ae 
poolse In the total city-wide program, there was a marked increase 
in the number enrolled in swimming classes, as well as in the number 
of awards granted in Y.I.C.A- tests from beginner to Life Saver 
proficiency = (623 persons were given swimming instruction and 622) 
passed tests.) 


IIT, 


PROGRAM (cont !d) 


In the fall, the Diamond Jubilee of basketball 
was celebrated at Central Branch, when news motion pictures 
were taken of games in "The Oldest House League in the World" 
now in its 60th veare 

Water Polo, Basketball and Volleyball teams under 
Y.M.C.A. colours brought honour to the Montreal Association 
in Dominion and Provincial Championship play. 


Summer Program — City Day Camps: 

n terms of program, the summer season was anything 
but "quiet". Priority was very definitely given to concern 
for junior members, when 229 school boys and girls were enrolled 
in ten City Day Camps. The summer was ideal for the many outdoor 
activities which were carried on during July and August. Play= 
fields, picnic grounds and swimming pools were used to good 
advantage. Generally speaking, the City Day Camp program trend 
is towards family events, where parents have an opportunity to 
join with their children in holiday activities. Industrial and 
business firms were most cooperative in arranging educational 
tours for children, The Canadian Ordnance Depot at Longue Pointe 
again made available their grounds and outdoor swimming pool for 
regularly scheduled visits from children of three branches, Most 
Day Camps concluded with a Parents! Night, at which awards for 
various achievements were presentede 


Summer Camps - Kamp Kanawana; 
The summer of 1952 was ideal for campinge Registrations 


for Kanawana, our boys camp in the Laurentians near Ste Sauveur des 
Monts, started early and enrollment of campers for the first six 


weeks soon reached capacitye In all, 06 boys spent an average of 
8 weeks at camp between June 20th and August 2 rde Campers and 
staff will look back on 1952 as the year of the "Long House", 


Officially opened and dedicated in mid-July, this spacious waterfront

recreation hall was a great asset, especially for rainy weather 
program, with its large stone fireplace and stagee It also 
provides winter storage space for the entire camp flect of 50 
boats and canoes, and quarters for the waterfront directors 

Indian lore and council rings were popular in the program of 
bantam and junior sectionse Intcrmediates and seniors continually 
explored the Archambault River and Lake District on canoe trips 
and overnight hikese A four-page newspaper pictorial story of

Otoreke Camp: 
"The Y-M.C.A. Home in the North" opened its 59th season 


for young men and women on June lst and continued through Labour 
Day weekend. More than 50% registered as "former campers" and 
many spent several weckends at camp in addition to their regular 
holiday period. Committccs planned each week's program for campers 
which always featured Saturday night get-acquainted events and 
Sunday morning services held in the beautiful outdoor setting 

of Chapel Island, overlooking sparkling Lake St. Joseph and 
surrounded by tall Otoreke birchese. During the summer, the camp 
enrolled Sil men Q women and 52 married couples, making a total 
of 1195 campers, who came from parts of Greater Montreal and 
three lively groups from Ottawa, Rochester and Torontoe Six-day 
canoe trips into the area west of Lake Labelle have become so 
popular that plans are under way to sccure permanent camp sites in 
the areae On three difforent occasions, parties of thirty young 
people went out on canoe tripse In all, 12 campers took part in 
these weekly excursions, supervised by six capable leaders. Seven 
new cabins were built in 1952, to replace but not increase accom- 
modation for camperse 


Camp Perrot: 
This near-the-city camp opened its ninth season of six 
weeks for boys and tw weeks for girls with an almost complete change 


of staff and counsellors. A new set of wharves, an enclosed swimming 
area and five new sturdy boats were provided through a generous gift 

of the Foremen's Club of Montreal, and added greatly to the safety 

of the camp's swimming programe The planting of five thousand Norwegian 
spruce trees by boys and girls of Hi~Y Clubs was tho first step in 


Bo 


TIIe PROGRAM (cont'd) 


a long term reforestration plan for Camp Perrote An enrollment of 
205 boys and 103 girls, for an average stay of 2.2 weeks cach, made 

a_ capacity attendance for the eight-week period. The completely 
equipped Laddie Millen Memorial Handicraft Shop under the supervision of 
an expert director produced an outstanding craft program. The peak 
of excitement for each week of boys! camp was reached when campers in 
full war dress assembled at their India Council fires, held above the 
shores of lake Ste Louis, '"Papooses","'Braves" and "Warriors" pitted 
their strength and skills against each other, and tribal rivalry was 
keen in weekly competition, The three camp war canoes were in great 
demand by young explorers who covered the waters from Lachine to 
Carillon on overnight trips with their section directors. A popular 
innovation in the girls! camp program was the replacement of morning 
assembly by candlelight evening vesper services, closing each busy 
day with counsellors! voices carolling through the camp after "lights 
oute" 


Christieville Ski Lodge: 

The Ski Club enrolled 140 members. Sleeping quarters at 
the Laurentian Y.M.C.A. lodge were taxed to the utmost during 16 week- 
ends, and the overflow of enthusiastic skiers were accommodated at 
nearby farmhouses, During the season there was an aggregate attendance 
of 1100. Three ski tows were operated near the lodge, and beginners 
classes were held throughout the season, An operating committee of 15 
men and women took charge of cross-country runs, a ski meet and 
carnival,and a number of special events for club members. 


Social Recreation: 

Not only in organized Young People's Social Clubs are 
friendships fostered and strangers made to feel at home in the Y.M.C.Ae 
Due in part to the influence of the SomEd type of program, the trend 
towards a social hour at the close of an evening's program is becoming 
increasingly evident. Square Dancing Clubs and Hoe-Dovms have become 
popular in many branchese Westmount Branch has led the way in providing 
instruction for "callers". 

A mid-winter conference of representatives from each of 
the Teen Social Clubs inthe various branches was held to discuss topics 
related to the program and operations of these popular clubs for boys 
and girlse Social activities for boys and girls up to fourteen years 
of age generally took the form of separate parties at Halloweten, 
Christmas, and such occasionse It is interesting to note that attend~ 
ance at dances, parties and social affairs, and at motion pictures have 
decreased, in contrast with marked increase in all other program arease

SIR GEORGE WILLIAMS COLLEGE AND SCHOOLS 
ee ne ae SEES, 


Growth continued in the College and Schools, in 
spite of the fact that the capacity has been apparently taxed 
to its maximum for several years, particularly in the Evening 
Divisions 

Several factors have made this possible. An 
additional "annex" was added during the year, with the conversion 
of the house at 131 Drummond Street to classrooms, bringing to 
five the number of buildings in use by the College in addition 
to the main Y.M-C.A. building. The Evening High School expanded 
its program to include 19 new classes on Saturday mornings. 
Moreover, the advanced classes in the Evening College, which 
have been gradually building up since the first degrees were 
awarded in 1936, are now approaching capacity, but their continued 
growth in 1952 made some increase in numbers possible. 

Although the College proper ( the Faculties of Arts, 
Science and Commerce) have shown the most spectacular growth in 
recent years, the Schools continue to develop, particularly the 
Evening High School which is serving a larger registration than 
ever before in its history. 

Total enrollment in the College and Schools in the 
academic year 1952-53 reached 655, of whom 3550 were in the 
College proper, and 2995 in the Schoolse In addition there were 
1897 students enrolled in the Summer Session, making a total 
service load of 842 during the academic years This year's 
enrollment represents an increase of 709% over last years The 
distribution of registration was as follows:

In addition, there was qualitative advancement during 
the years Several of the academic departments were strengthened 
by the appointment of additional, full-time faculty, particularly in 
Physics and Mathematics. The staff of the Student Oounsellor's 
department, which continues to play an important role in the service 
of the College and Schools, was augmented and its program expanded. 
Particularly noteworthy in this department during the year was the 
growing importance of the remedial reading program, the mental hygiene 
services and the work of the placement officer provided by the 
National Employment Services 

At the annual Convocation of the College held in June 1952, 
there were awarded 292 Bachelor's degrees in Arts, Science and Commerce, 
together with 22 Associate Diplomas and four Diplomas in Association 
Science. In addition,39 othor persons qualified for degrees as a 
result of the September examinationse At the graduation ceremony of 
the Evening High School, 107 graduation diplomas were awarded and )6 
certificates of graduation from the Evening Elementary School. The 
Business School awarded 35 complete graduation diplomas during the 
year, and a larger number of partial certificates. 

The staff of the College and Schools now numbers 30, 
persons, of whom 7h are full-time employees, and 230 part-time teachers y 
in addition to about 23 laboratory demonstrators and other assistants. 

The year in the College was one of buoyant hope, and an 
expectancy stimulated by the efforts which was under way to provide 
a new and more adequate building. For more than 25 years the major 
problem continuously facing the College had been one of space and 
facilities. Temporary solutions had been successively outgrown, and 
still a growing need had continued to challenge the College and the 
Montreal Y.M.C.A. 

As long ago as 1873, the Y.M.C.A+ of Montreal began offering 
evening educational opportunities for working pcoplee The purpose of 
the College still is, as stated in its By-Laws, "to give effect to the 
purposes of the Young Men's Ohristian Association of Montreal through 
the medium of formal education, and related activiticse" Toward this 
end, 1952 was a successful yeare 


Ve 


PERSONAL SERVICES 


Residences: 

More than a thousand young men applied for residence 
at the Y.M.C.A- last years ‘or many of these, it has been their 
first home in Canada, At Central, Westmount and International 
Branches, there has been a constant demand for the 622 beds 
available in residences. In Central Branch, where the greatest 
demand has been felt, new policies have been effective. There 
has been a shortening of the length of stay for transients, an 
increase of available double accommodation, and help given to 
secure suitable accommodation elsewhere. All residence members 
have been encouraged to take part in Y.M.C.A+ programs of their 
choice, and a great number of them have done sos Five issues of 
the "Resi~News", published in mimeographed form by a number of 
capable young men, served to acquaint residents with membership 
privileges, and to foster a spirit of friendship in the Central 
Branch residences 


Interviews and Employment : 
oung people constantly seek counsel and guidance 

in a multiplicity of perplexing problems confronting them in their 
daily lives. They turn to the Y.M.C.A- for understanding help 
regarding family relationships, making friends, use of leisure 
time, educationalyvocational and religious problemse These are 
some of the concerns that have formed the content of 58,460 personal 
interviews recorded in the Y.}.C.A- during the past yeare In Sir 
George Williams College alone, 1500 students sought personal 
counselling in "Student Personality Services", in addition to 
the large number of young men and women who automatically come 
within the range of counselling services as new college studentse 

Many hundreds of young men and women scek advice 
concerning their life work, cither in searching for their first 
job or in attempting to improve or change to work for which they 


are better suited. Last year, 990 employment placements were made.

OUR CHRISTIAN EMPHASIS 


"The Y.M.CeA. is a world-wide fellowship united 
by a common loyalty to Jesus Christ for the purpose of building 
Christian personality in a Christian society." 

This is our fundamental purpose. The Association, 
through its many and varied activities, recognizes its responsibility 
and opportunity in helping young people mould their lives on 
strong spiritual values, in a world where spiritual and material 
forces struggle for their allegiance. Because of its broad 
membership constituency and because it touches the lives of young 
people at so many vital points, the Y.M.C.A. is able to be an 
outstanding influence for religious unity. Through the 
encouragement of group service projects, it attempts to give 
members experience and training in making decisions and undertaking 
responsibility based on Christian principles, 

During the past year, members and staff have on many 
occasions conferred to evaluate program in the light of current 
needs of youth and our Ohristian objectives, In branch spring and 
fall program planning conferences, and at City-Wide Staff Training 
sessions, there has been concern for interpreting and strengthening 
our Christian faith, 

The beautiful Chapel in the Central Building has been 
open daily for meditation, and has been used consistently throughout 
the year for many club induction ceremonies, for Worship services, 
and special Christmas, Easter and Lenten services of staff and members 
BroupSe 

The Association observed the International Y.M.C.Acg 
YeleCoA- Week of Prayer, with a wide distribution of devotional 
literatures

of 2123 over the total at the same date a year ago. This substantial 
increase took place in Sir George Williams College enrollment and 
in Notre Dame de Grace, International, Point St. Charles, Lachine 
and Northmount Branchese

COMMUNITY -WIDE COOPERATION 


The Association has endeavoured to work in close 
relationships with homes, schools and churches, and with all 
community organizations vitally interested in the welfare of 
youths 

Through Parents! Nights, family banquets, lectures, 
forums and discussion groups, and through the many comnittce 
and club meetings held in homes, the Y.M.C.A. has fostered 
a close relationship with the home. 

We have continued to endeavour to cooperate with 
schools by supplementing school programs with school-centered 
clubs, by organizing sports and leagues, particularly in 
communities where school facilities have been made available 
for Y.M.C.A. offices and program, by participation in home 
and school associations, and by the increased use of our 
building facilities in programs for school children, such 
as Learn—to-Swim Campaignse 

Cordial relations with churches have been main= 
tained. On many occasions, our facilities have heen used by 
various Church groups for program such as Young People's socials, 
Sunday School Swims, and picnics at campe The Y.M.C.A., affil- 
iated with the Canadian and World Councils of Churches, partic- 
ipated in the formation of a looal Council of Churches, 

We have had helpful cooperative relationships with 
many other bodies. It is impossible to list them all in this 
report. Facilities in our buildings were granted to 2 


organizations during the year, 1835 meetings were held, attended 
by an estimated 89,371 personse

POLICY AND SURVEY COMMITTEE 


The Policy and Survey Committee appointed in 199 
"to study our present branches, Sir George Williams College 
and Schools, in relation to the needs of their respective 
communities to recommend new areas which require Y.M.C.A. 
services and adjustments in areas now served; to study present 
buildings operated by the Association and their adequacy to 
meet the needs and recommend structural changes required; 
to consider what new buildings may be required and to prepare 
estimates of annual maintenance costs involved in the recommend= 
ations," completed its task. 

The following brief interpretive comments on the 
final report indicates the trend of the observations and 
recommendations. 

"A thorough study of fees and general membership 
problems is needed, and further assistance and coordination 
should be given on a Metropolitan level in such matters as 
program, public relations, and leadership recruiting and 
trainings" 

Establishment of some procedure whereby lay officers 
of Branch Boards of Management can exchange ideas on common 
problems similar to the methods used in connection with the 
Secretarial Cabinet is desirable. 


Drumnond-Stanley Building: 

Central Branch = needs additional handball courts, 
adequate arts and crafts and club rooms and additional locker 
room spaces 

Metropolitan Offices ~ need additional office space

FINANCE AND PROPERTY 

Early in January, it was decided to hold a Capital 
Funds Campaign in November to implement the report of the Policy 
and Survey Committee and secure funds for annual maintenance 
requirements. 

The combined objective including campaign expenses 
was set at $3,300,000 and Mr. John B. Frosst accepted the General 
Chairmanship of the appeale 

Because of the magnitude of the task and the fact 
that the appointment of a General Secretary was still pending, 
it was felt advisable to engage the services of John Price Jones 
Company (Canada) Ltde, which firm had already directed three large 
capital funds campaigns in Montreal, 

Organization work commenced in March and continued 
through to the public phase of the appeal November 16 = 27, with 
the following citizens accepting leadership responsibilities as 
indicated: 


Honorary Chairman ~ del’e McConnell 

Honorary Vice-Chairmen - John Bassett, L.J+ Belnap, 
G.W. Bourke, Harold Crabtree, 
SeGe Dobson, 8B.Ce Gardner, 
ReH-e McMaster, R.E. Powell, 
J.Ms Pritchard, GeA. Walkers 

General Chairman - John Be Frosst 

General Vice-Chairmen - T.H. Atkinson, H.M. Long, 
L.W. Townsend, F.B. Valls, 
C.W. Webster. 


Chairman Advance Corporations - JeA- Fuller 
Chairman Advance Individuals - deH.Fe Turner 
Chairman Special Men - T. Denton Lewis 
Chairman Commerce & Industry ~ B.l. Roberts 
Chairman General Corporations - AH. Cowie 
Chairman Y.M.C.A- Branches - dJeJ.Fe Bancroft 
Chairman Public Relations - Murray R. Chipman 


Sixty-four citizens representing different aspects of 
civic life sponsored the appeal as members of the Citizens! Committees 


Mebe 


196 


FINANCE AND PROPERTY (cont'd) 


The Y.M.C.A+ Branches organization of fifteen divisions 
each under capable leadership did a very thorough job of covering 
approximately 20,000 prospects in the general canvasse 

The Sir George Williams College participated as a 
separate segment of the campaign for the first time and undertook 
to canvass students, alumni and faculty, a total constituency of 
77006 

All aspects of the publicity were very efficiently 
handled and combined to keep the constituency well informed and 
aware of the needs of the appeale 

The opening dinner was held in the Mount Royal Hotel 
with Dre Eugene E, Barnett, General Scoretary of the National Council 
of the YMCA's of the UeS.A- as special speaker,e The meeting was 
well attended and helped a great deal to set the tone of the public 
appeale 

The Campaign had two phases = an advanced solicitation 
and a public canvass. Advance Corporations, Advance Individuals 
and Commerce and Industry segments. Meticulous and detailed consid= 
eration was given to rating and assignment,and many prospects 
required a great deal of attention. The work of Mr. J.A- Fuller, 
MreJeHeF+ Turner and Mr. B.l/. Roberts and their associates is to 
be heartily commended and the results showed ample evidence of a 
thorough going jobe 

The General Chairman, Mr. John B. Frosst, worked tire- 
lessly for many months in this major undertaking and at the final 
meeting of the public phase of the campaign, reported a total of 
29790, 328 from 14,295 donors. Efforts are continuing to realize 
the maximum potential by a careful follow-up of all possible sources 
of supporte 

In addition to routine decorating and repairs, the 
following major items of building maintenance were completed at a 
total cost of $15,000: 

Drummond~Stanley Building: redecorating two gymnasiums, 
rewiring main gymnasium. Renewing iron treads in basement stairs, 
and replacing four electric panel boxes, replacing side walls in 
boilers. 

International: replastering ceiling over swimming poole

Tab. FINANCE AND PROPERTY (cont'd) 


Southwestern: renewing parquetry floor in auditorium 
and major redecoratings 

Notre Dame de Grace: equipment replacements and repairs 
and redecorating and purchase of Graveley Tractor. 

Kamp Kanawana: replacement of kitchen stove, new roof 
on gallery and new steps at the Lookout; new roof on Dining Hall and 
Kitchen; repairs to foundations of Hospitals 

Provision was made for the future development of Y.M.C.A- 
facilities in Lachine by the acquisition of seven lots comprising 
approximately 25,000 sqefte on Provost and 39th Avenues. 

During the year the Association also took further steps 
to acquire additional property necessary for expanded facilities of 
the Sir George Williams College. Accordingly through its nominee, the 
Montreal Trust Company, property and buildings at 1423-27-31 Drummond 
Street were purchased with consummation of the transaction to take 
place on June 1, 1953. The carnings from these properties are adequate 
to defray operating costs and interest on invested capitale 


Legacies & Bequests: 
The outstanding leadership vhich the late President of the 
Association, Gerald W. Birks, gave to youth through the Y.M.C.A+ is 


vividly illustrated by the provision he made for perpetuating this 
interest. The Association received from the Estate during the year a 
bequest of $11,750 in cash and securitics which sum will be used to 
augment the funds received in the Capital Funds Campaign and has been 
included in the total announcede 

The formal acknowledgement of the Metropolitan Board of 
Directors is expressed in the following Resolution: 

"Resolved that the Young Men's Christian Association of 
Montreal place on record its sincere gratitude for the extremely 
generous bequest received from the Estate of the Late Gerald Walker 
Birks who gave such long and distinguished service and continuous 
financial support to the Associations 

That we advise the Exccutors of the Estate of our heartfelt 
appreciation of this further helpful action of our late President by 
vihich he has perpetuated his life-long interest in the welfare of youthe" 

Other bequests received during the year are recorded with 
appreciation: 

The sum of ‘500 from the Estate Mrs. Mary Luddington related 
to a deep interest in the North Branch some years agoe 

A legacy of $1000 from the Estate Toufic Sabra who for 
many years was actively interested in the work of the International 
Branch on Ste Catherine St.Easte

Park Lake Couchiching in August and Montreal took an active

"The Future Role of the Y.M.C.A. in Camda and the Secretary's

and later served as resource people for the Couchiching 
Conferences 


NATIONAL COUNCIL 


Our Association contributed $13,400 in support of 
the services of the National Council of Y.M.C.Ae's of Canada, 
of which we are a constituent member. Those services have 
included helpful periodic visits of Council staff. 

A Special Fall Physical Training week for Fellowship 
Sutdents was given by We McVicar, the National Secretary for 
Physical Education. 

Early in the year, a commission was established to 
study National Council purposes, goals and methods. Mr. George 
M. Hobart, of our Metropolitan Board of Directors, was 
appointed to serve on the Commission, for which the Montreal 
Association was asked to prepare a brief, 


XII, 


2he 


WORLD SERVICES 


Since 1889, the Y.M.C.A.'s of North America 
have assisted the establishment of indigenous Y.M.CeAe 
movements in overseas countries. Today support is given 
to the Y.M.C.A. in twenty-nine of the cighty nations of 
the world in which the Association is functioning. The 
latest additions to the list are in Ethiopia and Kenya 
in the rapidly-awakening African continent. 

Each year the need for the continuance of this 
work becomes more indispensible, and the International 
Committee of Y.M.C.i.'s is constantly pressed with urgent 
calls for assistance in new areas of strategic importancee 
The survival of democracy in large areas of the world is 
at stake today, and the Y.M.C.A. is in the forefront of 
the struggle. 

We were fortunate in Montreal to have four 
World Services secretaries as visitors in 1952: Arata Ikeda, 
National Boys' Work Secretary of Japan; Dr. Wilson Hume, 
the recently-retired Associate General Secretary of the 
National Council of Y.M.C.A.'s of India, Pakistan, Burma 
and Ceylon; Dr. LeE. Aplin, General Secretary of the Y.sM.CeAe 
of Beirut, Lebanon; and M.G. Dharmaraj, General Sccretary 
of the Y.M.C.A., Nagpur, India. All made excellent impressionse 
Mr. Dharmaraj, in particular, because of his lengthy stay 
in Montreal on a Fellowship, made an important contribution 
to the life and program of our Associatione In his time with 
us from December 1951 until April 1952, Mre Dharmaraj addressed 
dozens of meetings in our branches, and talked privately to 
hundreds of personse His attractive personality and his 
sincere Christian message will be a lasting influence among 
both the staff and the members, 

In funds raised, a new high mark was achieved, 
although the full now objective was not quite reached. The 
special needs project raised ‘3,500 for the Nagpur Hostel 
in India, and $350 for the Beirut, Lebanon, Y.MsCeAey 
contributed by the Syrian community in Montreal.

The World's Alliance of Y.M.C.A.'s, with head= 
quarters in Geneva, Switzerland, is the federating body which 
unites twenty-eight national movements, of which Canada and the 
United States each are members, The Alliance serves as a co 
ordinating body and is officially recognized by the United Nations 


as a consultative body. 


Its quarterly publication, World Communique, reached 


approximately 500 Montreal homes in the yeare 


It is strongly 


ecumenical in tone and is considered by many to be outstanding 


in its advocacy of world-wide Christian cooperations

OBITUARY 


It was with sorrow that we record the passing 
of Mr. A.M. Brown on March 2nd, 1952. Mre Brown rendered 
devoted service to youth through his long years of Christian 
service as an outstanding layman and board menber of the 
Lachine Branche Appointed Chairman of the Board of Management 
in 191, he held that position until his sudden deaths 


APPRECIATION 


We are mindful of the loyal support we have 
received from many persons and groups of perons, whereby 
our service to the youth of our community has been immeasurably 
strengthened and inspired. 

We are deeply grateful to all Officers, Board 
and Committee members, to hundreds of volunteer leaders for 
their interest and loyal service; to the daily and weekly press, 
and to radio stations for their generous support in publicizing 
our programs for youths to the Protestant School Board, for 
their generosity in making available school facilities for 
our programs; to the many churches and service clubs for their 
interest and supports; to the Montreal Council of Social Agencies, 
of which our Association is a corporate member; to the Religious 
Education Council; to the railways and other corporations; to 
our sister organization, the Young Women's Christian Association, 
and to the Young Men's = Young Women's Hebrew Associationg and 
the Quebec Federation of Youth Organizations, To the_staff of 
Secretaries and all others who have served the Association, 
we extend our gratitude. 


XVI. 


27° 


CONCLUSION 


The foregoing is the record of the work and 
life of the Montreal Young Men's Christian Association, 
told within the limits of words and figurese Much more 
dramatic, important and permanent are the impressions 
recorded on the personalities of the thousands of boys, 
girls and young people who have bcen active mombers and 
participants in the Association during the yeare In its 
constant endeavour to work helpfully with the youth of 
Montreal, and to assist in the development of Christian 
persons, the officers and leaders of the Y.M.C.Ae have 
kept constantly in mind the purpose of the movement. The 
Association has romained flexible enough in its organiz— 
ational structure and policies to enable adjustment and 
changes to take place in keeping with the growth of the 
metropolitan area of Montreal and the needs of youthe 

As we move into the second century of the 
Association service with youth, we are reminded of the 
necessity of being sensitive to the purposes of Almighty 
God and of constantly seeking His guidances 


Respectfully submitted, 


Fred Ge Hubbard, 
General Secretary

AUODIZOR St REPORT 


The Young Men's Christian Association of Montreal, 
Montrealse 


We have examined the Balance Shect of The Young 
Men's Christian Association of Montreal as at December 31, 1952, 
and the related Statement of Income and Expenditure for the year 
ended that date. In comection therewith we made a test examin- 
ation of the books of account and financial records of the 
Metropolitan Office and of the reports from the branches and from 
the Residence Building but we did not make a detailed audit of 
the transactions of the Association for the year. We have received 
all the information and explanations we have required. 


The inventories of books, foodstuffs and sundry 
supplies have been certified to be correct by the officers of 
the Association. 


In our opinion, based on the examination made, the 
attached Balance Sheet and related Statement of Income and 
Expenditure correctly set forth the financial position of the 
Association as at December 31, 1952, and the results of its 
operations for the year ended on that date, according to the best 
of our information and the explanations given to us and as shown 
by the accounting records examined by use 


PeSe ROSS & SONS 


Chartered Accountants.

REPORT 
OF 
THE NOMINATING COMMITTEE 
TO THE ANNUAL MEETING OF THE 
YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION OF MONTREAL 
MONDAY, APRIL 13TH, 1953 


Mr. President: 


Your Committee, having carried out the constitutional 
requirements in connection with its duties, hereby nominates the 
following active members to become Directors of the Association: 


THe Atkinson Eric A. Leslie Howard I. Ross 
Joseph Me. Breen John Ge McConnell 0.B. Thornton 
Leslie H.T. Clegg James D. McKeown L.W. Townsend
